title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text: Case study · Methods · Results & evidence · Español · All projects

title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text:
El problema
¿Cómo selecciona y adapta el alumnado sus estrategias con fracciones? ¿Qué razonamientos se hacen visibles durante una actividad y cuáles quedan recogidos en una evaluación escrita?
Este TFG de Educación Primaria de la Universidad Rey Juan Carlos combina diseño de investigación, instrumentos de evaluación, análisis cuantitativo y observación cualitativa. Su aportación profesional está en cómo se obtiene e interpreta la evidencia.

title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text:
Diseño
Una clase de 22 escolares completó el cuestionario inicial. Se formaron tres estratos de competencia y se sortearon cinco participantes por estrato para el seguimiento detallado: 15 en total.
La secuencia comprendió cinco sesiones semanales: cuestionario inicial, tres sesiones con FracciChef, Dominó Fraccionario y FraccUNO, y una sesión final con juego libre y cuestionario posterior. No hubo grupo de control ni seguimiento diferido.

title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text:
Resultados y alcance
En los 15 participantes, la media del cuestionario pasó de 14,27 a 16,93 sobre 20; la mediana pasó de 14 a 17. Trece puntuaciones aumentaron y dos se mantuvieron en el máximo. El TFG reporta una prueba de Wilcoxon con W = 0 y p bilateral = 0,001. El archivo original de JASP no está disponible; estos valores se atribuyen al TFG y no se presentan como un análisis reproducido de forma independiente.
De 270 valoraciones de criterios durante el juego, 188 se codificaron como espontáneas. Son medidas repetidas de 15 participantes, no 270 observaciones independientes. Las rúbricas difieren entre juegos y sus totales no constituyen una escala común de progreso.
Las observaciones cualitativas sugieren que el formato de evaluación puede influir en el razonamiento que se logra registrar. Esto plantea una pregunta de investigación; no demuestra por sí solo un sesgo general de las pruebas escritas.

title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text:
Limitaciones
El diseño no permite atribuir la mejora exclusivamente a los juegos. La muestra es pequeña, pertenece a una sola clase y se selecciona según puntuaciones iniciales. Hay posibles efectos techo y regresión a la media, distinto tiempo de evaluación pre y post, observación de la propia investigadora e instrumentos sin validación psicométrica formal. El resumen metodológico y el anexo recogen listas de criterios parcialmente diferentes; por ello, no se publican rúbricas ni registros por criterio.

title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text:
Competencias demostradas
Diseño de investigación; elaboración de instrumentos; muestreo estratificado; estadística descriptiva; contraste no paramétrico; codificación cualitativa; triangulación; análisis crítico; comunicación de resultados.

title: Flexibilidad matemática en Educación Primaria
text:
Documentación y privacidad
La versión principal en inglés contiene el caso completo, la metodología y las notas de evidencia y disponibilidad de datos. Este resumen español no es una traducción íntegra de todas las páginas.
El repositorio incluye figuras generadas a partir de tablas agregadas del TFG. No incluye el PDF original, registros individuales, diagnósticos, citas del alumnado, fotografías ni documentación firmada. El código de figuras se ha creado después para el portfolio y no se presenta como código del análisis original.

title: Study methods
text: Case study · Methods · Results & evidence · Español · All projects

title: Study methods
text:
Design and sampling
The thesis describes an exploratory, descriptive mixed-methods study with qualitative emphasis and a single-group pre-post comparison. A class of 22 pupils completed the baseline questionnaire. Baseline score strata contained 7, 9 and 6 pupils; five were selected by lottery within each stratum for follow-up (N = 15).
The strata were formed from the observed distribution, with tied scores kept together. They are approximate competence groups rather than three equally sized thirds or external diagnostic cut-offs. Equal allocation to these groups does not make the follow-up sample proportional to the class. Neither stratification nor lottery selection is random assignment to an intervention.

The original framework calls the questionnaire evidence “potential flexibility” and observed performance “practical flexibility”. The written items also assess fraction knowledge and explanation, so the portfolio does not treat the total score as a fully validated, pure measure of flexibility. Xu et al.’s original measurement work concerns equation solving; transferring that framework to primary-school fractions requires validation.

Scope of the observation data
The methods summary and Appendix 5 list partly different observation criteria. This portfolio therefore presents only session-level strategy-origin counts as reported in Table 4.1. It does not reconstruct criterion-level records or offer a downloadable assessment rubric. The three games used task-specific instruments, so their totals are not treated as a shared scale of progress.

title: Study methods
text:
Quantitative analysis
The thesis reports medians and ranges alongside auxiliary means and standard deviations. The pre-post contrast is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, two-sided, with alpha = 0.05 and zero differences excluded. Group-level comparisons are descriptive only.
The test concerns paired differences, not the equality of means. The small sample, bounded score scale, tied differences and classroom context constrain interpretation. Neither a small p-value nor an effect-size label establishes educational effectiveness.

title: Study methods
text:
Qualitative analysis and integration
The source describes a thematic process informed by Braun and Clarke, with broad flexibility dimensions and strategy-origin categories set in advance. It is best described here as a combination of predefined analytical axes and inductive interpretation, rather than entirely inductive coding.
Written questionnaires, rubric ratings and field notes were interpreted together. Agreement can strengthen an interpretation, while disagreement may point to task demands, measurement limitations or contextual differences. Divergence alone does not identify which instrument is correct.
The thesis reports that a placement tutor reviewed observations concerning five participants across the three game sessions. This is a qualitative checking procedure, not a formally quantified inter-rater reliability study.

title: Study methods
text:
Reporting scope
The thesis reports research ethics approval. This portfolio presents whole-sample summaries and newly drawn illustrations. It excludes school identity, participant codes, diagnostic cross-tabulations, individual quotations, photographs, completed questionnaires and the original ethics certificate.

title: Study methods
text:
Selected references
These works inform the thesis; listing them does not imply that they validate every interpretation in this adaptation.

Xu, L. et al. (2017). Measures of potential flexibility and practical flexibility in equation solving. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1368. Article.
Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. DOI. Bibliographic details transcribed from the thesis; full text was not retrieved during the portfolio audit.

title: Evidence & data availability
text:
Statistical reporting
The source reports W = 0, p = 0.001 (two-sided), z = 3.18 and r = 0.58. It explicitly defines r = z / sqrt(N), with N = 30. That arithmetic gives about 0.581.
Some paired-test implementations use the number of pairs instead. The rstatix documentation specifies that convention. Using the same reported z with 15 pairs would give approximately 0.821; excluding the two zero-difference pairs from the denominator would produce another value. These are denominator illustrations, not replacement effect estimates.
Accordingly, the portfolio does not label r = 0.58 as an independently replicated result or promote it as a headline effectiveness claim. Because the original JASP project is unavailable, its calculation settings, tie handling and any continuity correction could not be verified. A normal approximation and a conditional exact calculation need not yield the same p-value.
The private audit reconstructed paired scores from Table 4.3 to check descriptive summaries. That is a new verification activity performed for this adaptation, not analysis code recovered from the original research. No paired records are included in the portfolio files.

title: Evidence & data availability
text:

Included: a Python standard-library script that reads transcribed aggregate CSV files, checks totals and creates three SVG figures. This is figure-generation reproducibility.
Not included: the original participant dataset, JASP project, item-level questionnaires, criterion-level ratings, coding files or field notes. The original statistical and qualitative analyses cannot be fully replicated from this repository.
The aggregate inputs are real thesis summaries, not synthetic pupil data. No synthetic dataset is used.

title: Making mathematical thinking visible
text:
Research design
Question: What strategies become visible in multiple-solution fraction games, and how do written scores differ before and after the sequence?
I combined a pre-post comparison with observation and qualitative records. A class of 22 pupils completed the baseline questionnaire. Five participants were selected by lottery within each of three baseline competence strata, producing a 15-participant follow-up sample.



Five sessions combined written assessment with classroom observation.









Evidence source
What it contributed




Written questionnaires, scored out of 20
Fraction knowledge, representations and explanations before and after the sequence


Six-criterion rubric for each game
Structured evidence of reasoning within each activity


Strategy-origin codes
Whether a strategy appeared spontaneously or following prompting

Context for interpreting numerical patterns and differences between formats



The approach was mixed-methods, with qualitative emphasis. Written scores, observation and field notes were interpreted together. Sampling, instruments and analysis decisions →

title: Making mathematical thinking visible
text:
Inside the intervention
I designed three games to create more than one valid route to a solution. The aim was to make procedure choice, representation and adaptation observable.

01 / Procedural emphasis

FracciChef



Illustrative game mechanic: two quarter cards or one half card can satisfy a recipe requiring two quarters.


Players combine ingredient cards to complete a recipe. Different equivalent combinations make it possible to observe which route a player chooses and how they justify it.



02 / Representational emphasis

Dominó Fraccionario



Illustrative equivalence: a half-shaded rectangle and the symbolic fraction two quarters represent the same quantity.


A valid connection depends on equivalent quantities across visual and symbolic forms. Matching values requires looking beyond identical notation.



03 / Strategic emphasis

FraccUNO



Illustrative choice: a blue half card can be followed by a blue three-quarters card through colour, or a red two-quarters card through equivalent value.


Players can have several legal moves. Choosing between a colour match and an equivalent value creates an opportunity to explain and adapt a strategy.


The diagrams above are newly drawn explanations of documented rules, not reproductions of pupil work or the original card artwork. Each game was observed in one session, so game mechanics, rubric and order cannot be separated analytically.

Tools and scope: the original thesis reports JASP 0.18 for numerical analysis. Quarto and the Python aggregate-figure script were added later for this portfolio. The script regenerates figures from transcribed summaries; it does not reproduce the full original analysis.

title: Making mathematical thinking visible
text:
Interpretation & next study
The study documents higher written scores after the sequence and a range of strategies during play. Its broader contribution is a research process that considers both performance and how evidence of performance is collected.
This exploratory study describes a change within one classroom. The absence of a control group, differences between assessment conditions and the short follow-up limit the conclusions. Study limitations and measurement details →
A stronger next study would combine a comparison group, delayed follow-up, harmonised assessment conditions and independent observation. Full methodological limitations →

title: Gamification & Commercial Success in Educational Math Apps
text:
Incorporating game mechanics (gamification) is one of the most common design responses in educational apps. But which mechanics, if any, are actually associated with commercial success (downloads) of primary-school math apps on the Google Play Store? And is popularity a reliable signal of pedagogical quality?
This is an observational, cross-sectional study. All results describe statistical associations, not causal relationships.

And is popularity a reliable signal of pedagogical quality?

title: Gamification & Commercial Success in Educational Math Apps
text:
Data & methods







Stage
Detail




Source
Google Play Store Apps (Kaggle, gauthamp10, 2021), ~2.3M raw records


Cleaning
Deduplication, null handling, Rating Count > 0, numeric coercion


Target population
4,218 educational math apps via a precision-oriented semantic keyword filter (validated recall gap ~6.4%)


Sampling
Stratified random sampling on log10-downloads; 4 quartile strata; n = 200 (50 per stratum); design weights near-uniform (~21.09), so unweighted OLS is unbiased for the population


Coding
5 binary gamification variables coded by manual interface inspection; inter-rater reliability via Cohen’s kappa (κ = 0.831 after reconciliation)


Model
OLS, log-level form; HC3 robust standard errors; Halvorsen-Palmquist correction for dummy variables


Diagnostics
VIF, Breusch-Pagan, Shapiro-Wilk + Q-Q, Cook’s distance


Robustness
Bootstrap (1,000 resamples), exact Fisher test, re-estimation without influential points, Bayesian-shrinkage hyperparameter sensitivity



The five gamification mechanics: Levels, Rewards, Ranking, Avatars, Feedback. Controls: Price, adjusted Rating (Bayesian shrinkage), Advertising, In-app purchases (IAP).

title: Gamification & Commercial Success in Educational Math Apps
text:
The data at a glance
Before modelling, two patterns are worth seeing directly.






Figure 1: Full gamification is the exception: 47% of the 200 apps implement none of the five mechanics, and only 5% implement four or five.









Figure 2: Gamification mechanics tend to be adopted together (strongest correlation r = 0.56, Levels and Feedback) but stay well below severe collinearity; adjusted rating correlates negatively with downloads (r = -0.35).

Reading of the headline finding. Only reward systems are significantly associated with downloads. Applying the Halvorsen-Palmquist correction, (10^0.986 - 1) * 100 works out to about +870%, meaning apps with reward systems are associated with roughly 9.7x the downloads of comparable apps without them, holding the other factors constant. Levels and Ranking behave as hygiene factors (Herzberg): so standard that their presence no longer differentiates.

title: Gamification & Commercial Success in Educational Math Apps
text:
The code (illustrative)
The full, ordered scripts live in /R. Two representative excerpts:
Bayesian shrinkage estimator for perceived quality
vi <- apps$`Rating Count`; Ri <- apps$Rating
C  <- mean(Ri, na.rm = TRUE)
m0 <- quantile(vi, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
apps$Rating_Adj <- (vi / (vi + m0)) * Ri + (m0 / (vi + m0)) * C
Model I with HC3 robust standard errors
model_I <- lm(LogMaxInstalls ~ V_Niveles + V_Recompensas + V_Ranking +
                V_Avatares + V_Feedback + Price + Rating_Adj +
                ADS_bin + IAP_bin, data = apps)
coeftest(model_I, vcov = vcovHC(model_I, type = "HC3"))

title: Gamification & Commercial Success in Educational Math Apps
text:
Takeaways

For developers: invest in well-integrated reward systems and a freemium model; levels and rankings alone no longer move the needle.
For educators: download counts are not a quality signal, since the best-rated apps tend to be niche tools with small, loyal audiences.
Limitation: store metrics capture commercial reach, not learning. Measuring real educational impact would need longitudinal usage data.
